prompt: A real, sharp astrophotograph of the sky seen from the surface of an airless moon during an eclipse: the Earth passing in front of the Sun, high in a flat black sky. Wide 16:9 frame. The Earth is a perfectly round, completely black disc about one quarter of the frame height across. It sits high and right of centre, its centre about one third of the way down from the top edge and about three fifths of the way across from the left. The Sun is hidden just behind it, slightly to the left of the disc's centre, so all the light comes from the left side. The one distinctive detail: a hair-thin ring of deep copper-red and amber light, the sunlight bent through Earth's own atmosphere, traces the entire edge of the black disc. It is thickest and brightest on the left, where it swells into a short bright bead, and thins to a faint copper thread on the right. Beyond the disc, the Sun's corona extends as fine, fibrous, pearl-white streamers and straight rays reaching out about one disc-width, longest and brightest to the left and along a roughly horizontal axis, shorter to the right. They are made of distinct filaments, not a soft round halo, and they fade cleanly into the black before reaching the lower third of the frame. The black disc is flat black with no surface detail and no lift. The only light in the frame comes from the copper atmospheric ring and the corona. The sky: pure neutral black, unexposed, flat from corner to corner, with no gradient and no colour cast. No stars at all. The bottom third of the frame is completely empty, unbroken black: no ground, no horizon, nothing in it, with no streamer reaching into it. The finish is a crisp, slightly grainy, real scientific photograph with true blacks and no gloss. No sun disc visible, no sun rays from a visible sun, no starburst, no lens flare, no bokeh, no chromatic fringing, no nebula, no Milky Way, no text, no labels, no arrows, no watermark, no spacecraft.

A real, sharp spacecraft photograph of the sky seen from the surface of an airless moon: one very thin crescent Earth hanging high in a flat black sky. Wide 16:9 frame. One hard, unfiltered sun lights it from the left, so only a narrow sliver along the left limb is lit, about one tenth of the disc, shaped like an opening parenthesis. The lit sliver is mostly bright white cloud with a little dim, desaturated blue ocean between the cloud bands and no clear coastlines. The terminator is sharp. The rest of the disc, the night side, is completely black, the same black as the sky, with no detail, no city lights and no lift. The one distinctive detail: a hair-thin, pale blue line of Earth's own atmosphere traces the lit outer edge and continues a short way beyond both tips of the lit cloud, so the horns of the crescent are drawn out into fine blue threads that are longer than the white crescent itself, then end cleanly in black. This blue line is very thin and does not spread into the surrounding black. The sky: pure neutral black, unexposed, flat from corner to corner, with no gradient, no grain and no blue, purple or brown cast. No stars at all, because the exposure is set for the sunlit crescent. The bottom third of the frame is completely empty, unbroken black: no ground, no horizon, nothing in it, left clear so a horizon can be laid in later. The Earth sits wholly in the upper two-thirds. The finish is a pristine, high-resolution digital capture with crisp edges, true blacks and no gloss. A real, sharp space-probe photograph of the sky seen from a small airless moon: one ringed planet like Saturn hanging high in a flat black sky. Wide 16:9 frame. The planet and its rings sit in the upper left of the frame, off centre, with the rings spanning a little under half the frame width and the outer ring's left tip well clear of the left edge. The rings are tilted open about twenty degrees, so they form a broad, flat ellipse. One hard, unfiltered sun lights the scene from the left and slightly in front. The one distinctive detail: on the right-hand side, behind the planet, the globe's own shadow falls across the rings and cuts a clean, sharp-edged black notch out of them, as if a bite had been taken, and the ringlets resume on the far side of it. All light, shading and shadows agree on a single sun from the left. The only soft glow allowed is a faint thin haze on the planet's lit limb, which belongs to the planet's own air. The sky: pure neutral black, unexposed, flat from corner to corner, with no gradient and no colour cast. No stars at all, because the exposure is set for the sunlit planet. The bottom third of the frame is completely empty, unbroken black: no ground, no horizon, nothing in it, and no part of the rings reaching into it.
